say.text: A 70 kg adult with 40% burns is on a crystalloid drip set at 700 mL/h, the formula's starting rate.
Three hours in, urine is 15 mL/h. What do you do with the rate?

choices.label: Keep 700 mL/h, since the formula has set it
Raise the rate by about a fifth, then recheck hourly
Cut the rate by a fifth to protect the kidneys
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Low urine means the tissues are under-filled, so the rate goes up.
The formula gave a starting point. The urine tells you each hour whether to keep going.

choices.label: Sure of this? Skip the why

say.text: That choice is not right. Once the sum is worked, the rate feels settled, so leaving it alone looks sensible.
The formula is an estimate to check against urine output, and this patient's urine is 15 mL/h. Look at that number before you decide.

sure_note.text: You were sure of this one. A formula gives a starting rate; it does not replace reading the patient. Check the urine each hour.

say.text: That choice is not right. Cutting fluid when output falls looks careful, as if the kidneys were being protected.
Low output means the tissues are short of perfusion, so the volume is too low, not too high. Work out what low output says about the fluid already in.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction. Low urine signals under-perfusion, which reverses the sign of the adjustment.

say.text: Read the urine as a gauge of perfusion, not of how much the patient is losing.
What does a low reading tell you the tissues are short of?
Low urine means under-perfusion, so the rate goes up by about a fifth. Recheck the urine each hour and move the rate with it.
The formula is a starting estimate, not a prescription to hold.
The Parkland formula gives a number from weight and burn size.
Why is that result only a starting estimate?

choices.label: Needs vary with depth, delay and inhalation, so urine guides them
The formula is exact, so only a miscalculated sum needs correcting
It covers 8 hours only; the rest follows a protocol rate
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The sum is set by weight and burn size, but real need moves with depth, delay and the airway.
Hourly urine output tracks that movement, so it is what you titrate to.
That choice is not right. Once the sum is done, it feels like a prescription to deliver, which makes the formula look exact.
Depth, delay and inhalation injury change how much fluid the patient needs, and the sum leaves all three out.
That choice is not right. A protocol rate for the rest of the day sounds tidy, so the formula seems to run on its own.
The rate is re-set every hour from the urine, through all 24 hours, not fixed at a protocol figure.
What else about the patient, apart from the size of the burn, changes how much fluid they need?
Fluid need varies with burn depth, delay before resuscitation and inhalation injury. The sum is a start.
Hourly urine output guides the rate.
A 20 kg child has a 25% scald.
What hourly urine output do you aim for?

choices.label: 10 mL/h, half a mL per kilogram per hour
30 to 50 mL/h, the usual adult range
20 mL/h, about 1 mL per kilogram per hour
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. In a child the target is per kilogram, and it is higher than the adult figure.
Twenty kilograms at about 1 mL/kg/h gives about 20 mL/h.
That choice is not right. The adult target is half a mL per kilogram, so halving it for a child feels like the standard rule.
Children have smaller kidneys and a higher metabolic rate, which pushes the per-kilogram target up, not down. Work from the child's weight.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction for a child. The per-kilogram target is higher than the adult one.

say.text: That choice is not right. The adult range is the number most people remember, so it feels like a safe default.
The adult figure is for an adult's body and kidneys. A child's target is set by the child's kilograms.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age qualifier: the adult range does not transfer to a child.

say.text: Two things change for a child: body weight and the kidneys. Which of these should set the number?
A child's target is about 1 mL/kg/h. At 20 kg that is about 20 mL/h.
The adult 0.5 mL/kg/h and the 30 to 50 mL/h range do not transfer to a child.
A 70 kg adult has an electrical burn and dark, pigmented urine. Rhabdomyolysis, muscle breakdown, is suspected.
What hourly urine output do you aim for?

choices.label: 30 to 50 mL/h, the routine adult target here
75 to 100 mL/h, a higher target to flush pigment
20 mL/h, the usual figure for a child
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The aim is a higher urine flow to clear myoglobin, which overrides the routine adult figure.
That choice is not right. The routine target is the number you already know, so it is the easy default when a burn is in front of you.
Electrical injury with rhabdomyolysis needs more urine flow to clear myoglobin from the kidneys. The routine target does not cover that.
That choice is not right. The child figure was the last rule you used, so it feels like a pattern to repeat.
This is a 70 kg adult. The weight rule for children does not decide the target here; the reason for the infusion does.
Ask what the target is for here: matching a routine, or clearing pigment from the kidneys?
Electrical injury with myoglobinuria needs about 1 to 1.5 mL/kg/h, around 75 to 100 mL/h in an adult, to flush out pigment.
Alkalinising the urine is not routinely needed if the output is adequate.
A junior charted a 3-year-old's total body surface area (TBSA) as 30% by the adult rule of nines.
What is wrong with that figure?

choices.label: The adult chart is the standard, so 30% stands at any age
Children are small adults, so the same proportions hold
A child's head and legs carry different shares of the total
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A child's head and legs carry different shares, so adult sums mis-state a child's burn.
Re-estimate the burn before you calculate any fluid.
That choice is not right. The adult chart is the one everyone learns first, so it feels like the default for any patient.
Adult values are fixed for an adult body. A child's proportions differ, so the same chart gives the wrong share.
That choice is not right. A child looks like a small adult, so the same proportions feel close enough.
Proportions change with age. Ask which body parts change most between a child and an adult.
Which parts of the body are proportionally larger or smaller in a 3-year-old than in an adult?
A child's head is larger, about 18%, and each leg smaller, about 14%, than the adult figures.
The adult chart overstates the legs and understates the head. Re-estimate with a Lund and Browder chart before you set the fluid.
A 50 kg adult has a 40% burn and reaches you two hours after the burn. The ambulance has run 1,000 mL of Ringer lactate.
What rate do you set for the rest of the first 8 hours?

choices.label: 500 mL/h, the 3,000 mL left over six hours
670 mL/h, the full 4,000 mL over six hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Half the 24-hour total is due in the first 8 hours from the burn, and fluid already given counts toward it.
Run only what remains.
That choice is not right. The full first-8-hour total is the number you just worked out, so it feels like the figure to run now.
The 1,000 mL already in counts toward that total. Ask how much is still owed before you set the rate.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the subtraction: fluid given before arrival is part of the first-8-hour volume.

say.text: Start from the first-8-hour total, then ask how much of it the patient has already had.
Half of 4 × 50 × 40 is 4,000 mL due in the first 8 hours from the burn. Deduct the 1,000 mL given.
That leaves 3,000 mL over the six hours left, about 500 mL/h.
Two adults, both with 40% burns, start on the same rate. Patient A passes 12 mL/h of urine. Patient B passes 90 mL/h.
What does each need?

choices.label: Leave both at the formula rate
Raise B's rate and lower A's
Raise A's rate and lower B's
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Low urine means more fluid; high urine means less.
The same starting rate was split by what each patient's urine showed.
That choice is not right. When the numbers look ordinary, holding the starting rate is the easy default.
A starting rate is not a prescription. Two patients with opposite urine need opposite moves, so the rates must differ.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the starting rate: it is an estimate to be adjusted from urine output.

say.text: That choice is not right. More urine can look like more fluid going in, so high output seems to need more.
Urine is a gauge of perfusion, not of demand. Read each patient's number on its own and ask whether the tissues are full or short.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction: high output is a reason to reduce, because overload causes harm.

say.text: Read each patient's urine against the target. Which one shows tissues that are short of fluid?
Patient A's low output means under-perfusion, so A's rate rises.
Patient B's high output means B's rate comes down, to avoid overload.
A man's forearm is burned all the way round. Which description needs an escharotomy now?

choices.label: Full-thickness, all the way round, with the fingers going pale
Deep partial-thickness, all the way round, with blisters
Superficial red burn over the whole chest, breathing normally
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The full-thickness ring is what compromises the limb, and pale fingers signal it.
Release the eschar now.
That choice is not right. A deep burn that blisters looks severe, so depth seems to be the reason to cut.
Escharotomy is for full-thickness burns that encircle a limb and compromise its circulation. Check the depth qualifier first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the depth qualifier: escharotomy is for full thickness, not deep partial.

say.text: That choice is not right. A burn covering a whole chest feels like a crisis, so the size seems to demand a cut.
Size alone does not decide it. A superficial burn does not restrict the chest, so check the depth and the ventilation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check both qualifiers: depth and whether breathing is restricted.

say.text: Escharotomy releases a tight, unyielding crust. What must the crust be like, and what must it be doing to the limb?
Escharotomy is for circumferential full-thickness limb burns with distal ischaemia or falling pulses, and for chest burns that restrict breathing.
Incisions go through eschar only, along the midlateral and midaxial lines.
Why does a full-thickness ring of burn threaten the limb?

choices.label: Any deep burn forms eschar, so release it at once
Inelastic eschar constricts as swelling builds, compressing vessels
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The eschar cannot stretch, so swelling compresses the vessels. That is why the cut releases the pressure.
That choice is not right. Depth feels like the cause, because deep burns look like the dangerous ones.
A tight, inelastic eschar is what squeezes the vessels as oedema builds, not depth on its own. Ask what squeezes the limb.
Picture a tight, unyielding ring around a limb that is swelling inside it.
A full-thickness eschar does not stretch. As oedema builds under it, the eschar constricts the vessels and the distal limb is starved.
